slides.title: Variables and data types
slides.html:
Basics

Variables and data types

  • Use const by default
  • Use let only when the value will change
  • Avoid var (old, confusing scope rules)
  • Primitives: string, number, boolean, null, undefined
  • Objects and arrays hold groups of values

variables.js

const name = "Ada";        // string
let age = 21;              // number
const isEnrolled = true;   // boolean
let course = null;         // empty on purpose
let score;                 // undefined
 
age = age + 1;             // ✅ let can change
// name = "Bola"; // ❌ TypeError
 
const student = { name, age };          // object
const tracks = ["Backend", "Frontend"]; // array
 
console.log(typeof age);   // "number"

slides.title: Conditions and loops
slides.html:
Basics

Conditions and loops

  • if / else if / else to make decisions
  • Always compare with ===, not ==
  • Combine checks with && (and), || (or), ! (not)
  • for…of to loop over an array
  • while when you don't know how many times

conditions.js

const score = 72;
 
if (score >= 70) {
  console.log("Distinction");
} else if (score >= 50) {
  console.log("Pass");
} else {
  console.log("Try again");
}
 
const tracks = ["Backend", "Frontend", "Web3"];
for (const track of tracks) {
  console.log(`Track: ${track}`);
}

slides.title: Functions and arrow functions
slides.html:
Reusable code

Functions and arrow functions

  • A function is a named, reusable block of code
  • It takes parameters and returns a result
  • Arrow functions are a shorter way to write them
  • One-line arrows return automatically
  • Every Express route is an arrow function: (req, res) => { }

functions.js

// Function declaration
function greet(name) {
  return `Hello, ${name}!`;
}
 
// Arrow function
const add = (a, b) => a + b;
 
// Default parameter
const welcome = (name = "student") =>
  `Welcome to BlockHub, ${name}`;
 
console.log(greet("Ada"));  // Hello, Ada!
console.log(add(2, 3));     // 5

slides.title: Arrays: map, filter, reduce
slides.html:
Working with data

Arrays: map, filter, reduce

.map()

Transform every item into something new

.filter()

Keep only the items that pass a test

.reduce()

Combine all items into one value

.find()

Return the first item that matches

arrays.js

const students = [
  { name: "Ada", score: 82 },
  { name: "Tunde", score: 45 },
  { name: "Chi", score: 67 },
];
 
const names = students.map((s) => s.name);
// ["Ada", "Tunde", "Chi"]
const passed = students.filter((s) => s.score >= 50);
// [Ada, Chi]
const total = students.reduce(
  (sum, s) => sum + s.score, 0);
// 194

slides.title: Objects and destructuring
slides.html:
Working with data

Objects and destructuring

  • Objects store data as key: value pairs
  • APIs send and receive objects as JSON
  • Destructuring pulls values out in one line
  • Works for arrays too, by position
  • You will write this in every Express app:

const { email, password } = req.body;

objects.js

const user = {
  name: "Ada",
  email: "ada@mail.com",
  track: "Backend",
  address: { city: "Lagos" },
};
 
console.log(user.name);       // dot notation
console.log(user["email"]);   // bracket notation
 
const { name, track } = user; // destructuring
const [first, second] = ["Node", "Express"];
const { address: { city } } = user; // "Lagos"

slides.title: Three features you will use daily
slides.html:
Modern JavaScript

Three features you will use daily

Spread ...

Copy and merge arrays or objects without changing the original.

const base = { role: "student" };
const user = { ...base, name: "Ada" };
const all = [...frontend, ...backend];

Template literals ` `

Build strings with variables inside ${ }.

const msg = `Hi ${user.name}, you have ${count} classes`;

Optional chaining ?.

Read deep values safely. No crash if something is missing.

const city = user.address?.city;  // undefined, not a crash
const nick = user.profile?.nick ?? "Guest";

A server spends most of its time waiting.

Reading files, querying databases, calling other APIs. Async code lets Node keep serving other users while it waits.

slides.title: Callbacks
slides.html:
Async · step 1

Callbacks

  • A callback is a function you pass in, to be called later
  • Node's older APIs are built on callbacks
  • Output order is 1, 2, 3: Node does not wait
  • Error comes first: (err, data)
  • Nest too many and you get callback hell

callbacks.js

const fs = require("fs");
 
console.log("1. Start reading");
 
fs.readFile("notes.txt", "utf8", (err, data) => {
  if (err) {
    return console.log("Error:", err.message);
  }
  console.log("3. File says:", data);
});
 
console.log("2. I don't wait!");

slides.title: Promises
slides.html:
Async · step 2

Promises

  • A Promise is a value that will arrive later
  • Three states: pending, fulfilled, rejected
  • resolve() on success, reject() on failure
  • .then() gets the result
  • .catch() handles the error

promises.js

const getUser = (id) =>
  new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    setTimeout(() => {
      if (id === 1) resolve({ id, name: "Ada" });
      else reject(new Error("User not found"));
    }, 1000);
  });
 
getUser(1)
  .then((user) => console.log(user.name))
  .catch((err) => console.log(err.message));

slides.title: async / await
slides.html:
Async · step 3

async / await

  • async makes a function return a Promise
  • await pauses that function until the Promise settles
  • Reads top to bottom, like normal code
  • Only works inside an async function (or a module's top level)
  • This is how you will write almost all backend code

async.js

const showUser = async () => {
  const user = await getUser(1);
  console.log(`Found ${user.name}`);
};
 
showUser();
 
// Same result as:
// getUser(1).then((user) => console.log(...))
 
// What you'll write with MongoDB later:
// const user = await User.findById(id);

slides.title: try / catch / finally
slides.html:
Error handling

try / catch / finally

  • try: code that might fail
  • catch: handle the error instead of crashing
  • finally: always runs, success or failure
  • Throw your own: throw new Error("Invalid email")
  • An unhandled error can crash your whole server

errors.js

const showUser = async (id) => {
  try {
    const user = await getUser(id);
    console.log(`Found ${user.name}`);
  } catch (err) {
    console.log("Something went wrong:", err.message);
  } finally {
    console.log("Lookup finished");
  }
};
 
showUser(1);  // Found Ada
showUser(7);  // Something went wrong: User not found

slides.title: calc.js
slides.html:
Build · script 1

calc.js

  • process.argv is an array of what you typed
  • The first two items are the node path and the file path, so we skip them
  • Each operation is an arrow function stored in an object
  • Validate input before using it

$ node calc.js add 5 3
Result: 8

calc.js

const [, , op, a, b] = process.argv;
const [x, y] = [Number(a), Number(b)];
 
const operations = {
  add: (x, y) => x + y,
  sub: (x, y) => x - y,
  mul: (x, y) => x * y,
  div: (x, y) => (y === 0 ? "Cannot divide by 0" : x / y),
};
 
if (!operations[op] || isNaN(x) || isNaN(y)) {
  console.log("Usage: node calc.js <add|sub|mul|div> a b");
} else {
  console.log(`Result: ${operations[op](x, y)}`);
}

slides.title: lookup.js
slides.html:
Build · script 3

lookup.js

  • db is a fake database: an array of objects
  • setTimeout pretends the database is slow
  • await waits for the result
  • try/catch handles a missing student

$ node lookup.js 2
Found: Chi
$ node lookup.js 9
No student #9

const db = [{ id: 1, name: "Ada" }, { id: 2, name: "Chi" }];
const findStudent = (id) => new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  setTimeout(() => {
    const s = db.find((st) => st.id === id);
    s ? resolve(s) : reject(new Error(`No student #${id}`));
  }, 800);
});
 
const main = async () => {
  try {
    const s = await findStudent(Number(process.argv[2]));
    console.log(`Found: ${s.name}`);
  } catch (err) {
    console.log(err.message);
  }
};
main();
